summary:
Importance

One in 5 heart transplant candidates in the US die or are delisted without transplant. Donor hearts are currently allocated by a 6-status therapy-based system criticized for limited risk stratification and susceptibility to gaming.

Objective

To develop a new heart allocation policy based on an objective medical urgency score that ranks candidates based on the interaction between physiology and mechanical circulatory support.

Design, setting, and participants

Registry-based observational study using data from the US organ transplant system. All adult (aged ≥18 years) heart transplant candidates from January 2019 to August 2025 were included, split into training (2019-2023), validation (2023-2024), and test (2024-2025) datasets.

Main outcomes and measures

A marginal structural model of 6-week mortality without transplant was estimated (the US Candidate Risk Score [US-CRS]). Eight models were compared in held-out data by weighted time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and calibration by status. Finally, US-CRS was converted into an allocation policy and a match-run simulation of waitlist reordering was performed compared with the current 6-status system.

Results

Adult heart transplant candidates were partitioned into consecutive training (n = 21 859), validation (n = 7897), and test (n = 8256) datasets (mean [SD] age, 53 [13] years; 74% male). The chosen US-CRS model included 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable left ventricular assist device, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, and advanced mechanical circulatory support). In test-set cross-sections of candidates actively waiting on the same calendar date, US-CRS had similar or significantly higher time-dependent AUC than the current 6-status system (mean AUC, 0.807 vs 0.693, respectively) and acceptable calibration by status, especially for candidates who received their status by exception. In match-run analysis (n = 45 530 donor hearts), a US-CRS-based system led to 67% of transplant recipients moving down in rank order and increased observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate on the match run from 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system to 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under the US-CRS-based system.

Conclusions and relevance

In this registry-based study of US heart transplant candidates, a US-CRS-based allocation system prioritized sicker candidates with higher mortality without transplant compared with the current medical urgency statuses.
title: Development and Validation of an Adult Medical Urgency Score for US Donor Heart Allocation.

summary:
Importance

Patent protection allows pharmaceutical companies to charge high prices for prescription drugs during periods of market exclusivity, and their expiration usually defines when generic competitors can enter the US market. Patents on drug active ingredients are classified as primary patents, while patents on formulations, methods of use, and delivery devices are nonprimary.

Objective

To evaluate how pharmaceutical patent portfolios for US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drugs have evolved over time.

Evidence review

Patents on small-molecule drugs approved by the FDA from 1990 to 2019 were examined and assessed for changes in the number and types of patents per product. The additional duration of total patent exclusivity associated with each patent type was quantified, and how often patents of each type were enforced against generic manufacturers in litigation was determined.

Findings

The FDA approved 1981 small-molecule drugs during the study period, and manufacturers listed 10 940 patents on these drugs. The mean number of patents per drug increased from 2.1 in 1990 to 6.9 in 2019, driven primarily by nonprimary patents. The mean number of nonprimary patents per drug rose from 1.2 in 1990 to 5.6 in 2019. Nonprimary patents represented majorities of FDA-listed patents (84% [9236/10 940]) and litigated patents (87% [4586/5253]). Nearly all patents listed after drug approval were nonprimary (96% [4874/5064]), and these patents extended market exclusivity by a mean of 6.1 years (SD, 5.8 years) and a median of 4.7 years (IQR, 0.2-10.1 years).

Conclusions and relevance

Pharmaceutical patent portfolios have grown over the last 2 decades. These portfolios have largely been built on nonprimary patents, which are then enforced against generic firms at higher rates than primary patents. Large patent portfolios can complicate routine generic competition and prolong periods of high drug prices.
title: Patents on Small-Molecule Drugs Approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, 1990-2019.

summary: Nivolumab plus relatlimab is approved for advanced melanoma based on the RELATIVITY-047 trial; however, long-term data are needed. Here, we report data from RELATIVITY-047 with the longest follow-up at present. In this phase 2–3, double-blind trial, patients with metastatic/unresectable melanoma were randomized 1:1 to nivolumab 480 mg plus relatlimab 160 mg (n = 355) or nivolumab 480 mg (n = 359) intravenously every 4 weeks. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) by blinded independent central review. Secondary endpoints were overall survival (OS), response, and safety. Additional post-hoc analyses such as melanoma-specific survival (MSS), and exploratory biomarker analyses are also reported. This analysis shows clear separation in survival curves with the largest absolute differences to date in PFS, OS, and MSS. In this prespecified 5-year analysis, with a minimum follow-up of 57.3 months, nivolumab plus relatlimab demonstrated continued clinically significant benefit versus nivolumab for PFS (hazard ratio = 0.77; 95% confidence interval: 0.65–0.92), OS (hazard ratio = 0.78; 95% confidence interval: 0.64–0.95), and MSS (hazard ratio = 0.71; 95% confidence interval: 0.57–0.88). The safety profile remained consistent with prior reports. Among biomarker-evaluable patients in the programmed death ligand 1 ≥1% subgroup, analyses revealed an association between worse outcomes with nivolumab and high peripheral or tumor lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG-3)+ CD8 cell levels. The addition of relatlimab to nivolumab was associated with a lower prevalence of primary resistance than nivolumab alone. These data support the hypothesis that relatlimab can overcome LAG-3–mediated resistance to nivolumab and provides evidence for differential efficacy patterns observed across biomarker subgroups linked to primary versus acquired resistance states. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03470922. As presented at the ESMO Congress 2026: In a 5 year follow-up of survival and correlative data from the pivotal phase 3 RELATIVITY-047 trial comparing relatlimab plus nivolumab versus nivolumab alone in patients with metastatic or unresectable melanoma, statistically significant differences in progression-free survival, overall survival and melanoma-specific survival were seen with high baseline levels of LAG3 high CD8+ T cells associated with improved response in the combination arm.

summary:
Background

Trifluridine-tipiracil (FTD-TPI) plus bevacizumab is the standard treatment for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer. However, the conventional schedule is frequently associated with haematological and gastrointestinal toxicity, which is clinically significant and relevant to patients. A simplified 14-day schedule has been proposed to reduce toxicity, but whether this treatment preserves survival has not been established in a randomised trial. We therefore aimed to assess whether the 14-day schedule is non-inferior to the conventional schedule for overall survival.

Methods

PRABITAS was a pragmatic, multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3, non-inferiority trial conducted in 178 hospitals in Japan. Patients with refractory metastatic colorectal cancer were randomly assigned (1:1) using a minimisation algorithm, stratified by Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, RAS mutational status, and institution, to FTD-TPI (35 mg/m2 orally twice daily) plus bevacizumab (5 mg/kg intravenously) on either a conventional 28-day (FTD-TPI on days 1-5 and 8-12; bevacizumab on days 1 and 15) or 14-day schedule (FTD-TPI on days 1-5; bevacizumab on day 1). Eligibility criteria were broadened compared with those of conventional explanatory trials, and trial procedures were aligned with routine clinical practice. The primary endpoint was overall survival, analysed in the intention-to-treat population, with a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 1·25. Safety was assessed in all patients who received at least one dose. Missing data were not imputed. This trial is registered with the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials, jRCTs041230120, and is closed to enrolment.

Findings

Between Dec 26, 2023, and May 20, 2025, we randomly assigned 972 patients, of whom 970 (99%) constituted the intention-to-treat population after two were excluded because they were randomly assigned before site approval (486 [50%] to the 28-day treatment group, 292 [60%] men and 194 [40%] women]; and 484 [50%] to the 14-day treatment group, 264 [55%] men and 220 [45%] women). Median follow-up was 17·9 months (IQR 14·3-22·6). Median overall survival was 10·3 months (95% CI 9·5-11·6) in the 28-day group and 11·3 months (10·2-12·5) in the 14-day group (stratified hazard ratio 0·93 [95% CI 0·80-1·08]). The 12-month overall survival rates were 44·0% (95% CI 39·5-48·5) in the 28-day group and 47·5% (42·9-52·0) in the 14-day group. Neutropenia grade 3 or worse was reduced in the 14-day group (13% vs 39%; absolute difference 25 percentage points [95% CI 20-31]), as was anorexia grade 2 or worse (15% vs 26%; absolute difference 11 percentage points [6-16]). Two treatment-related deaths occurred in the 14-day group and none in the 28-day group.

Interpretation

A 14-day schedule of FTD-TPI plus bevacizumab was non-inferior to the conventional 28-day schedule for overall survival, while reducing haematological and gastrointestinal toxicity. These findings support this simplified schedule as the new standard for FTD-TPI plus bevacizumab in refractory metastatic colorectal cancer.

Japan Society for the Promotion of Science KAKENHI Grant-in-Aid for Challenging Research (Pioneering).
title: 14-day versus 28-day trifluridine-tipiracil plus bevacizumab for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer (PRABITAS): a pragmatic, multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3, non-inferiority trial in Japan.

summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports clinical decisions, but human oversight is protective only if clinicians recognize and resist erroneous output. We systematically reviewed controlled and real-world studies of clinician responses to incorrect automated advice. Forty-six reports represented 41 independent cohort clusters, including 40 core cohorts. Across three adjusted cohorts, clinician correctness was substantially higher with correct than incorrect automated advice (pooled OR 10.19, 95% CI 7.43–13.98; I² = 0%); a ≥ 2020 sensitivity analysis was similar but imprecise (OR 9.22, 95% CI 2.06–41.13). In four heterogeneous real-world computerized ECG studies, 26.6% of erroneous interpretations were not corrected or recognized (95% CI 6.4–65.6%; I² = 95.8%). Contemporary AI and large language model studies also documented harmful reliance but were too heterogeneous for pooling. Patient-level adverse events were reported in one retrospective cohort. Human oversight should be evaluated as an error-interception capability rather than assumed to ensure safety.
title: Human oversight of erroneous clinical AI and decision support a systematic review and meta analysis

summary: In patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) treated with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy, factors associated with efficacy overlap with prognostic biomarkers. Currently, there is no consensus on optimal product characteristics. We analyzed the phenotypic attributes of the anti-CD19 CAR T therapy axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) from 580 patients with NHL across multiple clinical trials with long-term follow-up (median, 41.9 months). summary: Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification Proposed Rule (CMS 9873-P) Introduction Consistent with the President’s goal to prevent waste, fraud, and abuse, today the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), issued the Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. This rule would align Exchange eligibility and verification regulations with new requirements specified under the Working Families Tax Cuts (WFTC) legislation (P.L. 119-21). The WFTC legislation amended the Internal Revenue Code to establish new eligibility requirements for the premium tax credit (PTC). The Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification proposed rule would establish new Exchange requirements that align advance payments of the premium tax credit (APTC) and cost-sharing reductions (CSRs) eligibility with PTC eligibility changes enacted under sec. 71303 of the WFTC legislation and proposed to be codified in regulations issued by the Department of the Treasury on October 15, 2026. Currently, when consumers apply for coverage through Exchanges, they provide certain information that Exchanges may attempt to verify electronically. If an Exchange cannot verify the information electronically, the consumer enters an inconsistency period during which they need to submit documentation to verify their information. Under existing policy established by the Affordable Care Act (ACA), Exchanges provide APTC and CSRs (collectively, financial assistance) during the inconsistency period to consumers who otherwise appear eligible. If they do not submit documentation to verify their eligibility before the end of the inconsistency period, APTC and CSRs are generally reduced or ended. The Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification proposed rule would require Exchanges to verify the following criteria before providing financial assistance: household income and family size status as a citizen, U.S. national, or eligible noncitizen (including lawfully present) eligibility for or enrollment in other qualifying coverage place of residence However, under the proposed rule, consumers could enroll in Exchange coverage without financial assistance during the inconsistency period while verifications are pending. It would also establish a verification period beginning August 1 before Open Enrollment (OE) each year to ensure that consumers have ample opportunity to provide and confirm information impacting their eligibility before the following coverage year. This proposed rule also includes provisions on annual eligibility redeterminations and re-enrollment, eligibility redeterminations during the plan year, timeline requirements for states seeking to transition to a State-based Exchange, binder payments, a waiver of the proposed verification requirements for certain Special Enrollment Periods (SEPs), effective dates for eligibility determinations, annual OE notices, and plan selection requirements. The proposed regulations would ensure financial assistance is only provided when income can be verified, potentially reducing the risk that consumers would have to repay excess APTC at tax filing due to inaccurate income estimates. They also would reduce improper or fraudulent enrollments by requiring verification of certain eligibility criteria before providing financial assistance, improving program integrity. The provisions in the Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification proposed rule would be effective starting with eligibility determinations made for plan year 2028. The rule would require Exchanges to make a pre-OE verification period available starting August 1 each year ahead of OE, during which consumers could choose to provide eligibility verification information earlier for next coverage year. The first pre-OE window would start August 1, 2027, for 2028 coverage. The Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification proposed rule is available on the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/2026-21891/patient-protection-and-affordable-care-act-exchange-pre-eligibility-verification . Stakeholders may submit public comments for a 30-day period following publication of the proposed rule. Strengthening Program Integrity Requiring Verification Before Receiving Financial Assistance CMS proposes new regulations for verification requirements for consumers requesting financial assistance for Exchange coverage. Exchanges would no longer be permitted to provide financial assistance during inconsistency periods when certain eligibility criteria cannot be verified electronically. Additionally, CMS proposes that Exchanges maintain or reduce the amount of financial assistance provided during such inconsistency periods after an enrollee voluntarily reports a change in circumstances that impacts eligibility for financial help. These new requirements would help ensure that only eligible consumers receive financial assistance. Requiring Annual Verification CMS proposes that currently enrolled consumers would only be automatically re-enrolled with financial assistance if they return to the Exchange to confirm certain eligibility criteria annually and have it re-verified by the Exchange. Consumers who don't actively return and have their information re-verified for financial help would be automatically re-enrolled without financial assistance. The new requirement would help ensure that only eligible consumers receive financial assistance through annual re-enrollment. Supporting Exchange Consumers Opportunity for Verification Before Open Enrollment Beginning August 1, 2027, CMS proposes that Exchanges provide consumers the option to submit certain eligibility information for the Exchange to verify before annual OE. CMS proposes requiring all Exchanges make this pre-OE verification period available to new and returning applicants to provide a minimum set of eligibility information and that all Exchanges start their annual pre-OE verification period on August 1 each year. By providing the early opportunity for verification, the proposed rule would help Exchange enrollees to have their eligibility fully verified before the upcoming coverage year, ensuring continuous coverage with financial assistance from year to year. Flexible Enrollment Options for Consumers CMS proposes requiring Exchanges to allow consumers to select a contingent plan during OE or a SEP such that the plan selection would become effective only if the consumer is determined eligible for financial assistance. This means consumers may choose a plan based on preliminary financial assistance estimates that would only start after they confirm eligibility for financial assistance. This process would enable consumers who elect not to enroll when they do not receive financial assistance during their inconsistency period to enroll once they are determined eligible for financial assistance, even if OE or their SEP, as applicable, has ended. Ensuring Timely Access to Financial Assistance CMS proposes new effective date rules for eligibility determinations and redeterminations made under the other proposed requirements in this rule. These proposals include new effective dates for financial assistance eligibility determinations and redeterminations after successful verification of eligibility. For consumers already enrolled in a health plan when their eligibility for financial assistance is verified, we propose providing financial assistance retroactively for the months during their inconsistency period when they were enrolled. For consumers who select a plan pending verification of eligibility for financial assistance, meaning the plan won’t start until after verification, we propose that their enrollment and financial assistance become effective and will start based on when their eligibility is verified. These proposed rules would provide clarity to consumers, Exchanges, and issuers; ensure timely access to coverage and financial assistance; and limit risks of adverse selection. Flexibility in Open Enrollment Notification Starting with plan year 2028, CMS proposes to permit Exchanges to provide the written annual OE notification to each enrollee before the pre-OE verification period, instead of in the month before OE starts. This would permit Exchanges to design the most effective outreach strategy to educate their consumers about the earlier verification period opportunity and the annual OE. Exception for Changes in Family Size CMS proposes waiving new verification requirements for consumers with certain changes in family size, as outlined in Treasury’s regulations, so that their financial assistance is based on their attested application information during inconsistency periods. This applies when a consumer or their household member qualifies for an SEP triggered by birth, adoption, marriage, or loss of a dependent through divorce, separation, or death (if allowed by the Exchange). Improving Exchange Rules Comment Solicitation on Enhancing Verification Procedures CMS seeks comment on how to strengthen Exchange requirements to verify family size and residency, including which data sources CMS should consider using or making available. CMS seeks comment on ways to increase program integrity while limiting burden on consumers and limiting operational costs and burdens for state and federal Exchanges. State Exchange Transitions CMS proposes that a state submits its application for HHS’ review and approval to become a State-based Exchange 15 months before a state begins operations as a State Exchange for the pre-OE verification period, instead of 15 months before OE. This would ensure the required pre-OE verification period is available to consumers when a State-based Exchange launches, removing the risk that a consumer first verifies on the Federally-facilitated Exchange (FFE) during the pre-OE verification period and then must reverify on the State-based Exchange. This requirement would ensure transitioning states align their transition timeline with the start of the pre-OE verification period, which would be the start of their operations as a State-based Exchange, instead of the start of OE. Binder Payment Alignment CMS proposes that the FFE and State-based Exchanges on the Federal Platform (SBE-FPs) must make prospective and retroactive enrollments under this proposed rule subject to the existing binder payment rules for prospective and retroactive enrollments, respectively. In addition, State-based Exchanges have the option to adopt the same changes. This would give issuers additional flexibility to set binder payment due dates for the proposed new enrollment scenarios. Effective Dates CMS proposes limited updates for current rules on effective dates for financial assistance eligibility redeterminations, when an existing enrollee reports a change to the Exchange during the coverage year. Specifically, in cases where the enrollee does not qualify for an SEP, CMS proposes no longer allowing Exchanges to delay effective dates for such eligibility redeterminations beyond the first of the month after the redetermination occurs. This change would align effective dates across existing and new scenarios and ensure timely eligibility updates. CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145

summary:
Importance

Trastuzumab rezetecan (SHR-A1811) has demonstrated encouraging antitumor activity in a global phase 1 trial involving heavily pretreated patients with erythroblastic oncogene B (ERBB2)-low metastatic breast cancer.

Objective

To compare trastuzumab rezetecan vs physician's choice of chemotherapy in patients with ERBB2-low metastatic breast cancer.

Design, setting, and participants

This open-label, randomized, multicenter phase 3 trial was conducted at 73 hospitals across China. Eligible patients were females aged 18 to 75 years with centrally confirmed ERBB2-low (immunohistochemistry [IHC] 1+ or IHC 2+/in-situ hybridization [ISH]-negative) unresectable locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer who had received 1 or fewer prior lines of chemotherapy for metastatic disease, with prior endocrine therapy required for hormone receptor-positive disease. Enrollment began on June 30, 2023, and ended on August 20, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the final analysis for progression-free survival in the current study was March 20, 2026.

Interventions

Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive trastuzumab rezetecan (6.4 mg/kg intravenously every 3 weeks; n = 277) or physician's choice of chemotherapy (n = 274).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary end point was progression-free survival assessed by blinded independent central review in chemotherapy-naive patients and the overall population.

Results

Between June 30, 2023, and August 20, 2025, a total of 551 patients were randomized, with a mean (SD) age of 54.9 (9.9) years. At the data cutoff (March 20, 2026), trastuzumab rezetecan significantly prolonged progression-free survival compared with chemotherapy in the chemotherapy-naive patients (median, 16.6 [95% CI, 14.0-19.4] months vs 6.8 [95% CI, 5.7-7.0] months; hazard ratio, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.19-0.33]; P < .001) and the overall population (median, 16.4 [95% CI, 14.0-16.8] months vs 6.8 [95% CI, 5.7-6.9] months; hazard ratio, 0.27 [95% CI, 0.21-0.34]; P < .001). The benefit was consistent in hormone receptor-negative disease (median progression-free survival: 16.5 vs 6.8 months; hazard ratio, 0.34, [95% CI, 0.22-0.54]) and hormone receptor-positive disease (median progression-free survival: 16.4 vs 6.7 months; hazard ratio, 0.24 [95% CI, 0.18-0.33]). Grade 3 or greater treatment-related adverse events occurred in 84.1% of patients (232/276) with trastuzumab rezetecan and 67.9% (184/271) with chemotherapy, most commonly decreased neutrophil count (180 [65.2%] vs 147 [54.2%]).

Conclusions and relevance

Trastuzumab rezetecan provided significant progression-free survival benefit over physician's choice of chemotherapy in patients with ERBB2-low advanced breast cancer, with benefit observed across all key subgroups. It exhibited the potential as a new treatment option with a distinct safety profile in this setting.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05814354.
title: Trastuzumab Rezetecan in ERBB2-Low Advanced Breast Cancer: The HORIZON-Breast06 Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Background

Remibrutinib is a highly selective, potent, covalent, CNS-penetrant, oral BTK inhibitor. We assessed the efficacy and safety of remibrutinib in adult patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis.

Methods

REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2 are two identical, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active comparator-controlled, parallel-group, event-driven, phase 3 trials conducted at 407 centres in 46 countries. Patients aged 18-55 years with relapsing multiple sclerosis, an Expanded Disability Status Scale score of 0-5·5, and evidence of recent disease activity were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily via interactive response technology. Randomisation was stratified by geographical region, MRI cohort participation, and multiple sclerosis subtype. Patients, site investigators, and trial team were masked to treatment allocation. The primary endpoint was annualised relapse rate (ARR), defined as the number of confirmed multiple sclerosis relapses per patient-year with up to 30 months of follow-up, and assessed in all randomly assigned patients. These trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05147220 and NCT05156281) and are ongoing, not recruiting.

Findings

Between Dec 13, 2021, and Dec 30, 2025, 2632 patients were screened and 2007 patients were randomly assigned. REMODEL-1 included 1000 patients (remibrutinib 502, teriflunomide 498; mean age 38·2 years, 666 [66·6%] female, 334 [33·4%] male) and REMODEL-2 included 1007 patients (remibrutinib 504, teriflunomide 503; mean age 39·0 years, 675 [67·0%] female, 332 [33·0%] male). ARR was significantly lower with remibrutinib than with teriflunomide: 0·073 versus 0·112 (rate ratio [RR] 0·648 [95% CI 0·453-0·927]; p=0·018) in REMODEL-1 and 0·080 versus 0·116 (RR 0·688 [0·487-0·972]; p=0·034) in REMODEL-2. The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (132 [13·1%] of 1006 with remibrutinib vs 137 [13·7%] of 1001 with teriflunomide), nasopharyngitis (92 [9·1%] vs 123 [12·3%]), diarrhoea (84 [8·3%] vs 109 [10·9%]), and alopecia (58 [5·8%] vs 135 [13·5%]). Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were less frequent with remibrutinib (31 [3·1%]) versus teriflunomide (58 [5·8%]). The safety profile of remibrutinib was consistent with that in other indications, including no liver safety concerns.

Interpretation

Remibrutinib was superior to teriflunomide in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, while maintaining a favourable safety profile. These findings support remibrutinib as a potential new oral treatment option for relapsing multiple sclerosis.

Funding

Novartis.

summary:
Background

In patients with IgA nephropathy, complement activation drives glomerular inflammation, which leads to hematuria, proteinuria, and nephron loss. Ravulizumab is a terminal complement inhibitor that prevents formation of C5a and C5b-9.

Methods

In this phase 3 trial, we enrolled adults with IgA nephropathy who had an estimated glomerular filtration rate of at least 30 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and proteinuria (24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio [with protein and creatinine both measured in grams] of ≥0.75 or total urinary protein excretion of ≥1.0 g per day), despite standard therapy. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive an intravenous infusion of either ravulizumab or placebo every 8 weeks. In the prespecified interim analysis, the primary efficacy end point was the change from baseline in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 34. Safety was also assessed.

Results

In all, 485 patients underwent randomization, with 240 patients assigned to the ravulizumab group and 245 to the placebo group; 352 patients (176 in each group) were included in the interim analysis. In the ravulizumab group, the geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at baseline and at week 34 was 1.56 and 0.83, respectively; in the placebo group, it was 1.60 and 1.48, respectively. At week 34, a significant reduction in the geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was observed with ravulizumab (-46.6%) as compared with the reduction observed with placebo (-5.6%), corresponding to an adjusted geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio that was 43.4% (99% confidence interval, 30.1 to 54.2) lower with ravulizumab than with placebo (P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 69.5% of the patients receiving ravulizumab and in 75.8% of those receiving placebo; serious adverse events occurred in 4.6% and 9.0%, respectively. No meningococcal infections or deaths occurred.

Conclusions

In adults with IgA nephropathy, ravulizumab resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo at week 34. (Funded by Alexion, AstraZeneca Rare Disease Unit; I CAN ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06291376; EU Clinical Trials number, 2023-507851-31-00.).
title: Ravulizumab in IgA Nephropathy - Interim Analysis of a Phase 3 Trial.

summary:
Background

B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) have distinct roles in IgA-producing B-cell populations and appear to be central to the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy. Povetacicept, an enhanced, variant transmembrane activator and calcium-modulator and cyclophilin-ligand interactor (TACI)-Fc fragment fusion therapeutic, is engineered for dual inhibition of BAFF and APRIL.

Methods

In this ongoing, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, participants with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy receiving stable background therapy were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive povetacicept at a dose of 80 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks. The primary end point of this prespecified interim analysis was the change in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 36. Secondary end points were the change at week 36 in galactose-deficient IgA1 levels and hematuria resolution at week 36 among participants with baseline hematuria.

Results

A total of 557 participants received povetacicept (372 participants) or placebo (185 participants). Efficacy analyses included the first 199 participants who had undergone randomization (131 in the povetacicept group and 68 in the placebo group). summary: People who become pregnant after living kidney donation may be at increased risk of pregnancy-related adverse outcomes, although the evidence is unclear. To determine whether pregnancies after living kidney donation are associated with a higher risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes than matched pregnancies among nondonors. This matched cohort study used provincial administrative health care databases from Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta, Canada, and included living female kidney donors aged 18 to 42 years who donated a kidney between July 1992 and August 2021 and subsequently had singleton pregnancies of at least 20 weeks' gestation. These pregnancies were matched 1:4 with singleton pregnancies of at least 20 weeks' gestation among female nondonors. Pregnancies in donors and nondonors were matched on delivery date, age at delivery, years between cohort entry and delivery, number of prior pregnancies, and income. Final follow-up occurred until March 2023. Outcome analysis occurred from August 2024 to September 2026. The primary outcome was a composite of hospitalization with a diagnosis of gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, or eclampsia. Secondary outcomes included 12 maternal, fetal and neonatal adverse outcomes, including the individual components of the primary outcome, the composite of low birth weight or preterm birth, and small for gestational age at birth. The sample included 385 pregnancies in 252 living kidney donors (mean [SD] age, 27.8 [5.0] years) matched to 1540 pregnancies in 1535 nondonors (mean [SD] age, 27.0 [4.8] years). The primary composite outcome of gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, or eclampsia occurred in 46 donor pregnancies (11.9%) and 128 nondonor pregnancies (8.3%; risk ratio, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.10-2.08). Among the 12 secondary outcomes, the 95% CI for the risk ratio excluded 1.00 for the outcome of small for gestational age, which occurred in 53 donor pregnancies (13.8%) and 121 nondonor pregnancies (7.9%) (risk ratio, 1.86; 95% CI, 1.37-2.52). In this study, pregnancy after living kidney donation was associated with a higher risk of the composite outcome of hospitalization with a diagnosis of gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, or eclampsia, when compared with matched pregnancies in nondonors. Most postdonation pregnancies were uncomplicated. These findings support counseling donor candidates who may become pregnant about this risk and informing the prenatal care of donors who become pregnant.

summary:
Importance

For patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), guidelines recommend considering maintenance therapy after achieving remission. Data comparing maintenance therapeutic options are limited.

Objective

To compare the effects of rituximab and azathioprine maintenance therapies on remission duration for patients with EGPA who recently achieved remission of vasculitis after standard therapy, including prednisone tapering or withdrawal.

Design, setting, and participants

From March 7, 2018, to June 2, 2022, this double-blind, double-dummy, investigator-initiated, superiority, randomized clinical trial enrolled 98 participants with EGPA from 36 hospitals in France. Inclusion eligibility required a new EGPA diagnosis or relapsing EGPA within 30 to 360 days of achieving vasculitis remission (Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score of 0 [range, 0-63, with higher scores indicating more severe disease activity]) after a standard induction regimen. Data were analyzed from April 1, 2025, to September 17, 2025. Additional analyses ended June 22, 2026.

Interventions

Participants were randomized to receive a predefined standardized tapering of oral prednisone and either 500 mg of intravenous rituximab every 6 months for 18 months and daily oral azathioprine placebo for 24 months (n = 49) or rituximab placebo every 6 months for 18 months and daily oral azathioprine for 24 months (n = 49).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary efficacy end point was the duration of total remission during the 28-month study period while taking 7.5 mg/d or less of prednisone. The 14 secondary end points included proportion of participants remaining in remission, rate of vasculitis relapse, and rate of asthma or rhinosinusitis exacerbations.

Results

All 98 randomized participants (mean age, 59.0 years [SD, 14.4]; 50 women [51%]) received at least 1 dose of the trial regimen and 92 (94%) completed the trial. The mean time in remission with prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less was 91.1 weeks (95% CI, 80.9-101.2) vs 96.0 weeks (95% CI, 85.6-106.5) in the rituximab and azathioprine groups, respectively (P = .38). The proportion of participants who remained in remission during the 28-month study period with prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less was 17 of 49 (34.7%) vs 11 of 49 (22.4%; relative risk, 1.51; 95% CI, 0.83-2.73; P = .18) in the rituximab and azathioprine groups, respectively. The proportion of participants with at least 1 vasculitis relapse was 7 (14.3%) vs 9 (18.4%) in the rituximab vs azathioprine groups, respectively, and for those with at least 1 clinically significant asthma exacerbation, rhinosinusitis exacerbation, or both, it was 16 (32.7%) vs 19 (38.8%). One participant in the azathioprine group died of SARS-CoV-2 infection before vaccine development. Rituximab recipients experienced a higher incidence of severe infections (23 [46.9%] vs 12 [24.5%], respectively), primarily due to severe SARS-CoV-2 infections.

Conclusions and relevance

For participants with newly diagnosed or relapsing EGPA, rituximab was not superior to azathioprine for improving the duration of total remission during 28 months while taking prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03164473.
title: Rituximab vs Azathioprine for Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Maintenance Therapy: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

Background

Sibeprenlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody, selectively inhibits the cytokine A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL), a key driver of IgA nephropathy. Preliminary trial results with regard to the primary end point of the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at 9 months after treatment as compared with baseline have been reported, but secondary end points, including outcomes regarding estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), have not.

Methods

We randomly assigned adults with IgA nephropathy to receive subcutaneous sibeprenlimab (at a dose of 400 mg) or placebo every 4 weeks. The key secondary end point was the annualized slope of the eGFR over 24 months. Other secondary end points included the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months, a composite kidney end point of kidney-function decline or kidney failure, and pharmacodynamic and safety end points.

Results

A total of 510 patients underwent randomization - 259 to receive sibeprenlimab and 251 to receive placebo. The annualized eGFR slope over 24 months was 0.3 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area per year (95% confidence interval [CI], -0.4 to 0.9) with sibeprenlimab and -4.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year (95% CI, -4.9 to -3.6) with placebo (between-group difference, 4.5 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.6 to 5.4; P<0.001). The least-squares mean treatment difference for the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months was 9.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, 7.1 to 11.4; P<0.001). A composite kidney end-point event occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) in the sibeprenlimab group and in 28 patients (11.2%) in the placebo group (adjusted difference, -10.8 percentage points; hazard ratio, 0.029; 95% CI, 0.004 to 0.214; P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 235 patients (90.7%) in the sibeprenlimab group and 226 patients (90.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 21 patients (8.1%) and 32 patients (12.7%), respectively; and serious infections in 5 patients (1.9%) and 10 patients (4.0%). No deaths were reported.

Conclusions

Among patients with IgA nephropathy, treatment with sibeprenlimab stabilized the eGFR slope over 24 months, a finding consistent with a reduced risk of kidney-function decline. (Funded by Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development and Commercialization; VISIONARY ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05248646.).

summary:
Background

Atacicept resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo in a previously published analysis of this trial, ORIGIN 3. Final prespecified efficacy results are reported here.

Methods

We randomly assigned adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy to receive weekly subcutaneous atacicept at a dose of 150 mg or placebo. We carried out final analyses of two secondary end points: the change in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at week 52 and the annualized eGFR slope through week 104; additional hierarchically tested end points and safety were assessed.

Results

Of 431 patients who underwent randomization, 428 received atacicept or placebo (214 per group). At week 52, the mean change in the eGFR was -0.11 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area (95% confidence interval [CI], -1.44 to 1.22) with atacicept and -5.69 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -7.04 to -4.35) with placebo (mean difference, 5.58 ml per minute per 1.73 m2; 95% CI, 3.68 to 7.48; P<0.001). Through week 104, the mean annualized eGFR slope was -0.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -1.62 to 0.41) with atacicept and -5.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -6.64 to -4.57) with placebo (difference, 5.00 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.55 to 6.45; P<0.001). Composite kidney-disease progression occurred in 11 patients (5.1%) in the atacicept group and in 38 patients (17.8%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.48; P<0.001); no patients in the atacicept group had progression to dialysis, transplantation, or death, as compared with 7 patients in the placebo group. Adverse events occurred in 160 of 214 patients (74.8%) in the atacicept group and in 167 of 214 patients (78.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 7.0% and 15.4%, respectively. One patient (in the placebo group) died.

Conclusions

Atacicept slowed and stabilized the decline in the eGFR as compared with placebo. (Funded by Vera Therapeutics; ORIGIN 3 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04716231.).
